name: Craft CMS 5
strengths: Exceptional content modeling — Matrix fields with nested entries, 23+ field types
Project Config — full config-as-YAML, git-friendly, environment sync
Built-in GraphQL API with GraphiQL IDE for headless mode
Core 2FA + Passkeys, account lockout, elevated sessions
Beautiful admin UI, live preview, Plugin Store with 1,000+ plugins
weaknesses: Commercial license — free Solo tier limited to 1 user
PHP/Yii — no TypeScript, smaller ecosystem than WordPress/Drupal
No native ETL/migration framework (Feed Me plugin only)
No advanced multi-step editorial workflows in core
No AI or personalization features built-in
bestFor: Design agencies, content-rich websites, digital experiences where content modeling and developer experience are paramount. Projects needing clean config management.
avoidIf: You need a free open-source license for teams, enterprise workflows, large-scale migration tools, or JS/TS stack.

name: Directus 11
strengths: Database-first — wrapper for any SQL database
Policy-based access control (v11) — very granular
REST + GraphQL + WebSockets (real-time)
Flows — visual automation builder
Full white-label branding, 30+ admin languages
weaknesses: Schema in DB, not in code — difficult config management
No faceted search, ETL, or migration framework
Content versioning — still maturing (breaking changes in v11)
Custom logic requires extensions (less flexible than hooks)
No routing/URL management (pure headless)
bestFor: Database-first projects, internal dashboards, data management tools. Teams wanting GUI-first approach with SQL database.
avoidIf: You need git-based config management, complex content workflows, or full-stack rendering.

name: Drupal 11
strengths: Most powerful content modeling system (entity/bundle/fields)
Views — visual query builder, no code required
Mature workflows: Content Moderation, Workspaces
Migrate API — enterprise-grade ETL
25 years of ecosystem, 50k+ modules
weaknesses: PHP — no TypeScript, harder JS stack integration
Steep learning curve for developers
Frontend (Twig) outdated vs React/Vue
Slower initial development (boilerplate)
More demanding hosting requirements
bestFor: Enterprise portals, governments, universities, large multilingual sites with advanced workflows and data migrations.
avoidIf: You have a small JS team, building SPA/mobile-first, or need a quick MVP.

name: Ghost 6
strengths: Best-in-class for publishing — clean, focused editor
Built-in membership, subscriptions, newsletter delivery
Content API + Admin API — clean headless architecture
Native analytics, SEO, and social features
Beautiful default themes, fast out of the box
weaknesses: NO multilingual support whatsoever
NO content versioning or revision history
Very limited content modeling — posts and pages only
No custom fields, no taxonomies beyond tags
No workflow system (draft/publish only)
bestFor: Professional bloggers, newsletter businesses, content creators, media publications focused on writing and membership monetization.
avoidIf: You need structured content modeling, multilingual, versioning, custom fields, or complex editorial workflows.

name: Joomla 6
strengths: Powerful ACL — most granular permission system in traditional CMS
Native multilingual with 70+ language packs
Full revision history with custom field versioning
Built-in publishing workflows with scheduling
Smart Search with finder plugin architecture
weaknesses: Smaller plugin ecosystem than WordPress
Admin UI less intuitive than competitors
Config management weak — schema in database
Headless API support still maturing
No TypeScript — PHP-only backend
bestFor: Multilingual community portals, association websites, e-government, projects needing fine-grained ACL without enterprise fees.
avoidIf: You need headless-first architecture, JS/TS stack, or the largest possible plugin ecosystem.

name: KeystoneJS 6
strengths: Elegant schema API — clean TypeScript
Granular access control (operation + filter + field)
Document field — rich text with embedded React components
Prisma ORM — solid data layer
Lightweight, minimalist
weaknesses: NO i18n — multilingual does not exist in core (issue #322 since 2018!)
NO revision/versioning system
Small ecosystem — no marketplace, few plugins
GraphQL only — no REST API
Slow development — no releases since May 2025
bestFor: Small-medium English-only projects with simple data models. Developers who love GraphQL and Prisma.
avoidIf: You need multilingual, versioning, REST API, or a rich plugin ecosystem.

name: October CMS 4
strengths: Built on Laravel — clean architecture, Eloquent ORM, Artisan CLI, Composer ecosystem
Tailor content modeling — YAML blueprints for custom types without code
Excellent admin UI — dark mode, white-label branding, drag-and-drop dashboard widgets
Plugin Marketplace with 1,000+ plugins for extensibility
Strong forms system — YAML blueprints with triggers, conditions, repeaters (enhanced v3.6)
weaknesses: Multilingual requires plugin (RainLab.Translate) — no core i18n
No content versioning or revision history in core
No AI features — no content generation, image, or translation capabilities
Limited API — no auto-generated REST or GraphQL, custom routes only
Commercial license — not standard open source (custom EULA since v2)
bestFor: Laravel developers building content-rich websites, agencies wanting clean admin UX with plugin extensibility, projects needing rapid development on a familiar PHP framework.
avoidIf: You need multilingual, content versioning, AI features, or a headless-first API architecture without custom development.

name: Payload CMS
strengths: TypeScript-first, code-as-config — full control
Native Next.js integration (same repo)
Granular access control at field/collection level (core)
Versioning, autosave, scheduled publishing in core
Lexical rich text editor — extensible
weaknesses: Young project — plugin ecosystem still growing
Documentation still evolving
Requires dev-first approach (no GUI schema builder)
No native search, facets, or ETL
API stability — rapid development = frequent changes
bestFor: Next.js developers wanting CMS + app framework in one repo. Projects where code control > GUI.
avoidIf: You need a GUI content modeler for non-technical users, or migrating from legacy CMS.

name: Strapi v5
strengths: Easiest start — GUI content type builder
Active community, plugin Marketplace
Draft & Publish + i18n in core
REST + GraphQL out of the box
Strapi Cloud — managed hosting
weaknesses: Review Workflows — Enterprise only (paid)
No native version history in Community
Limited search (no faceted, no abstraction)
Stability — v5 still maturing (70+ bugfixes in recent releases)
No scheduled publishing in core
bestFor: Startups, agencies, content hubs serving multiple frontends (web + mobile). Quick start for JS teams.
avoidIf: You need advanced workflows without Enterprise fees, or complex content migration.

name: Sulu CMS 3
strengths: Built on Symfony — full-stack framework with enterprise-grade architecture
Best-in-class multilingual + multisite (unlimited localizations per webspace)
Sulu.ai — multi-provider AI for content, translation, metadata (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepL)
Excellent SEO — core meta tags, sitemaps, canonical, hreflang, robots directives
Core content versioning, live preview, media library with focal point & crops
weaknesses: Small community — niche adoption outside DACH/European market
No ETL/migration framework — custom Symfony commands required
No 2FA, limited security features beyond Symfony defaults
Steep learning curve — requires Symfony expertise
Small plugin/bundle ecosystem compared to WordPress, Drupal, or even Craft
bestFor: Symfony developers building enterprise multilingual/multisite projects. Agencies in the DACH region needing content-rich, customizable websites with strong SEO and AI capabilities.
avoidIf: You need a JS/TS stack, large plugin ecosystem, quick MVP setup, or a platform with widespread community support.

name: TYPO3 14
strengths: Enterprise-grade content management — comparable to Drupal
Best-in-class multilingual (56+ languages, per-field translation)
Workspaces — full editorial workflow with staging
Complete revision history with visual diff and rollback
Granular caching framework with cache tags
weaknesses: Very steep learning curve — TCA configuration is complex
Smaller community than WordPress/Drupal (mainly DACH region)
Headless API requires extension (not core-first)
No TypeScript — PHP-only backend
Slower initial setup compared to headless CMS
bestFor: Enterprise portals in DACH region, large multilingual/multisite setups, organizations needing strict editorial workflows and governance.
avoidIf: You have a small team, need JS/TS stack, want headless-first, or need quick MVP.

name: Umbraco 17
strengths: Exceptional content modeling — Document Types, compositions, Block Grid/List editors
Core multilingual with per-property language variants and fallback chains (since v8)
Enterprise security — ISO 27001 certified, core 2FA, ASP.NET Identity, formal advisory process
Built-in Content Delivery API + Management API + webhooks for headless/hybrid mode (v12+)
Block Grid Editor — true drag-and-drop visual page building with custom blocks (v10.4+)
weaknesses: C#/.NET — no TypeScript, .NET expertise required, smaller open-source community than PHP CMS
SEO features require custom properties or packages — no core SEO tab
No AI features built-in — relies on community packages
Config sync requires uSync plugin or paid Umbraco Deploy — not core
No native GraphQL API — REST only
bestFor: .NET developers and agencies building enterprise websites, multilingual portals, and content-rich platforms. Strong fit for organizations invested in the Microsoft ecosystem.
avoidIf: You need a JS/TS stack, built-in SEO tools, AI features, GraphQL API, or a fully open-source solution with free config management.

name: Wagtail 7
strengths: StreamField — flexible, nestable content blocks with real-time preview
Built-in workflows — multi-step approval chains with custom tasks (since v2.10)
Excellent accessibility — dedicated a11y team, ATAG compliance, alt text enforcement
Full revision history with visual diff comparison and revert
Core multisite + i18n + REST API + search backends — versatile out of the box
weaknesses: Python/Django — no TypeScript, smaller ecosystem than WordPress/Drupal
No field-level permissions in core
Limited AI capabilities — only basic wagtail-ai package
No native visual page builder or inline editing (StreamField ≠ drag-and-drop)
No native GraphQL — requires wagtail-grapple plugin
bestFor: Python/Django teams building content-rich websites with structured editorial workflows, accessibility requirements, and multi-site needs. Strong fit for government, education, and non-profit sectors.
avoidIf: You need a JS/TS stack, visual drag-and-drop page building, field-level permissions, or a massive plugin marketplace.

name: WordPress 6.9
strengths: Largest ecosystem — 60k+ plugins, themes for everything
Easiest onboarding — everyone knows WordPress
Gutenberg block editor — powerful visual editing
Native revisions, scheduled publishing, media library
WP-CLI and massive community support
weaknesses: Multilingual requires plugins (WPML/Polylang — paid)
Security surface area — plugin quality varies wildly
Config management weak — schema lives in DB
Not truly headless by default (requires WPGraphQL plugin)
Performance at scale needs heavy caching/optimization
bestFor: Blogs, agency sites, small-medium businesses, content-heavy sites, anyone needing a quick setup with massive plugin ecosystem.
avoidIf: You need enterprise-grade workflows, strict config management, or a headless-first architecture.
